title: MOSFET & BJT Physics
description: Where the transistor equations come from: the MOSFET charge-sheet model, channel-length modulation, body effect and subthreshold conduction, and the minority carriers that set the gain of a bipolar transistor.

study.title: The charge-sheet model
study.body: Above threshold the gate induces an electron sheet $Q'_n = -C_{ox}(V_{GS} - V_T - V(y))$ under the oxide, where $V(y)$ is the channel voltage at position $y$ from the source. The current is constant along the channel: $I_D = W\mu_n|Q'_n|\,dV/dy$. Integrating from source ($V$ = 0) to drain ($V = V_{DS}$) gives the **linear** (triode) law. At $V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_T$ the charge at the drain end reaches zero (**pinch-off**) and the current saturates. With $k'_n = \mu_nC_{ox}$ and the overdrive $V_{ov} = V_{GS} - V_T$ this is exactly the first-year model $K = (W/L)(KP/2)$ with $KP = \mu_nC_{ox}$.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& I_D = \frac{k'_n}{2}\frac{W}{L}\left[2V_{ov}V_{DS} - V_{DS}^2\right]\\ & I_{D,sat} = \frac{k'_n}{2}\frac{W}{L}V_{ov}^2\\ & k'_n = \mu_nC_{ox}, \quad V_{ov} = V_{GS} - V_T\end{aligned}

study.title: Explore: output characteristics
study.body: $k'_n(W/L)$ = 2 mA/V² and $V_T$ = 0.5 V, curves for $V_{GS}$ = 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 V. The dashed parabola $I_D = \tfrac12 k'_n(W/L)V_{DS}^2$ separates the linear region (left) from saturation. Drag $\lambda$: **channel-length modulation** makes the saturated curves slope upward.

study.title: Mobility, $k'_n$ and transconductance
study.body: The electrons in the inversion layer scatter at the rough Si–SiO$_2$ interface and are pressed against it by the vertical field, so the **effective** channel mobility is well below the bulk value: typically 300–600 cm²/V·s for electrons. Example: $\mu_n$ = 500 cm²/V·s and $t_{ox}$ = 10 nm give $C_{ox}$ = 3.45$\times10^{-7}$ F/cm² and $k'_n$ = 173 µA/V². In saturation the transconductance grows linearly with the overdrive $V_{GS} - V_T$.

study.title: Channel-length modulation and body effect
study.body:
- **Channel-length modulation:** beyond pinch-off the depletion region at the drain grows with $V_{DS}$ and shortens the effective channel by $\Delta L$, so $I_D$ keeps rising slowly: $I_D \approx I_{D,sat}(1 + \lambda V_{DS})$, output resistance $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$. $\lambda$ is larger for short channels.
- **Body effect:** a source-to-body voltage $V_{SB} > 0$ widens the depletion layer under the gate, adding depletion charge, so the threshold rises:

study.title: Explore: subthreshold conduction
study.body: Below $V_T$ the current does not stop: it is a diffusion current over the source barrier, which the gate controls through the surface potential. The capacitive divider of $C_{ox}$ and the depletion capacitance $C_{dep}$ means only a fraction $1/n$ of a gate step reaches the surface, with $n = 1 + C_{dep}/C_{ox}$. The **subthreshold swing** $S$ (gate voltage per decade of current) is therefore at least $(kT/q)\ln 10$ = 59.6 mV/decade at 300 K. The curve uses a smooth interpolation (EKV form) between the exponential and square-law regions.

study.title: Short-channel effects
study.body:
When $L$ shrinks to the size of the depletion regions, the long-channel picture breaks down:
- $V_T$ **roll-off:** source and drain depletion regions take over part of the depletion charge, lowering $V_T$.
- **DIBL** (drain-induced barrier lowering): the drain voltage lowers the source barrier, so $V_T$ drops as $V_{DS}$ rises.
- **Velocity saturation:** the current saturates earlier and grows only linearly with $V_{GS} - V_T$: $I_D \approx WC_{ox}v_{sat}(V_{GS} - V_T)$.
- **Punch-through:** source and drain depletion regions merge; **hot carriers** damage the oxide.
Scaling therefore shrinks $t_{ox}$, the junction depths and the supply voltage along with $L$.

study.title: Explore: inside the bipolar transistor
study.body: In an npn transistor the forward-biased base–emitter junction injects electrons into the thin p-type base, where they are minority carriers; the reverse-biased collector junction pulls them out at $x = x_B$. With $x_B \ll L_B$ the electron profile is a straight line from $n_{B0}e^{V_{BE}/V_t}$ to about 0, so the collector current is a diffusion current set by its slope. Here $N_B = 10^{17}$ cm⁻³ ($n_{B0}$ = 2250 cm⁻³), $D_B$ = 20 cm²/s, $L_B$ = 20 µm. Drag $V_{BE}$ and the base width.

study.title: Current gain and the Early effect
study.body:
The common-base gain $\alpha_0$ is a product of factors below 1: the **emitter injection efficiency** $\gamma$ (how much of the emitter current is electrons injected into the base rather than holes injected back into the emitter; needs $N_E \gg N_B$), the **base transport factor** $\alpha_T$ (electrons that cross the base without recombining; needs $x_B \ll L_B$) and the junction recombination factor $\delta$. Then $\beta = \alpha_0/(1 - \alpha_0)$. For short emitter and base, $\gamma \approx 1/(1 + N_BD_Ex_B/N_ED_Bx_E)$ and $\alpha_T = 1/\cosh(x_B/L_B) \approx 1 - x_B^2/2L_B^2$.
**Early effect:** a larger $V_{CB}$ widens the collector depletion region into the base, so $x_B$ shrinks and $I_C$ rises: $V_A \approx qN_Bx_B/C'_{jC}$.

steps.title: A sheet of electrons
steps.body: Above threshold the inversion layer holds a charge $C_{ox}(V_{GS} - V_T)$ per unit area at the source. Towards the drain the channel voltage $V(y)$ rises, so less charge is induced there. The drain current is that charge moving with drift velocity $\mu_nE$. The process constant combines mobility and oxide capacitance.

steps.prompt: An NMOS process has an effective electron mobility of {{mu}} cm²/V·s and a {{t}} nm gate oxide. Find the process transconductance parameter $k'_n = \mu_nC_{ox}$.
An NMOS transistor has $k'_n$ = {{kp}} µA/V², $W/L$ = {{WL}} and $V_T$ = {{VT}} V. Find the drain current in saturation at $V_{GS}$ = {{VGS}} V (ignore channel-length modulation).

steps.title: Linear region and pinch-off
steps.body: For small $V_{DS}$ the channel is a voltage-controlled resistor. As $V_{DS}$ approaches $V_{GS} - V_T$ the inversion charge at the drain end goes to zero: the channel is **pinched off**. Electrons still cross the short depletion region at the drain, swept by its strong field, so the current saturates instead of stopping.

steps.prompt: An NMOS transistor ($k'_n$ = {{kp}} µA/V², $W/L$ = {{WL}}, $V_T$ = {{VT}} V) operates at $V_{GS}$ = {{VGS}} V and $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS}} V. Find $I_D$.
steps.explanation: $V_{DS,sat} = V_{GS} - V_T$ = {{VGS-VT}} V > {{VDS}} V, so the transistor is in the linear region. $I_D = \frac{k'_n}{2}\frac{W}{L}$ $[2(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS} - V_{DS}^2]$ = 0.5 × {{kp}}$\times10^{-6}$ × {{WL}} × ({{2*(VGS-VT)*VDS||3}} − {{VDS^2||3}}) = **{{0.5*kp*1e-6*WL*(2*(VGS-VT)*VDS - VDS^2)|A}}**.

steps.prompt: An NMOS transistor with $V_T$ = {{VT}} V has $V_{GS}$ = {{VGS}} V and $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS}} V. In which region does it operate?
steps.explanation: Compare: $V_{GS} - V_T$ = {{VGS-VT||3}} V. If this is negative there is no strong inversion: cutoff (only a small subthreshold current). Otherwise compare $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS}} V with $V_{DS,sat} = V_{GS} - V_T$: below it the channel reaches the drain (linear), above it the channel is pinched off (saturation).

steps.prompt: An NMOS transistor has $k'_n$ = {{kp}} µA/V², $W/L$ = {{WL}}, $V_T$ = {{VT}} V. Drag $V_{GS}$ until the saturation current is {{It}} mA (dashed line).
steps.explanation: $I_{D,sat} = \frac{k'_n}{2}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS} - V_T)^2$ gives $V_{GS} = V_T + \sqrt{2I_D/(k'_nW/L)}$ = {{VT}} + √(2 × {{It}} mA / ({{kp}} µA/V² × {{WL}})) = **{{VGSt|V}}**. The curve is flat beyond $V_{DS} = V_{GS} - V_T$ = {{VGSt-VT||3}} V.

steps.prompt: In saturation the channel is pinched off near the drain, yet the full drain current keeps flowing.
steps.explanation: Pinch-off only means the **inversion** charge vanishes at the drain end. Electrons arriving there are swept through the short, high-field depletion region into the drain, much like collector current in a BJT. The current is set by the channel up to the pinch-off point, which hardly changes with $V_{DS}$.

steps.title: Channel-length modulation
steps.body: In saturation the pinch-off point moves towards the source as $V_{DS}$ grows, shortening the effective channel. The current therefore rises slowly with $V_{DS}$, modelled by $\lambda$ (larger for shorter channels). The transistor's output resistance follows.

steps.prompt: Without channel-length modulation a saturated MOSFET would carry {{I0}} mA. With $\lambda$ = {{lam}} V$^{-1}$, what is $I_D$ at $V_{DS}$ = {{VDS}} V?
A saturated MOSFET carries $I_D$ = {{I0}} mA with $\lambda$ = {{lam}} V$^{-1}$. Estimate its small-signal output resistance $r_o$.
steps.explanation: $r_o = 1/(\lambda I_D)$ = 1 / ({{lam}} × {{I0}} mA) = **{{1/(lam*I0*1e-3)|Ω}}**. It limits the voltage gain $g_mr_o$ of a single transistor.

steps.title: The body effect
steps.body: If the source sits above the body ($V_{SB} > 0$), the channel–body junction is reverse biased by an extra $V_{SB}$. The depletion layer under the gate widens and holds more charge, which the gate must also support: the threshold rises.

steps.prompt: Find the body-effect coefficient $\gamma = \sqrt{2q\varepsilon_sN_a}/C_{ox}$ for $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³ and $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm (in V$^{1/2}$). ($\varepsilon_s$ = 1.035$\times10^{-12}$ F/cm)
An NMOS transistor has $\gamma$ = {{g}} V$^{1/2}$ and substrate doping $N_a$ = {{Na}} cm⁻³. By how much does $V_T$ rise when $V_{SB}$ = {{VSB}} V?

steps.title: Subthreshold conduction
steps.body: Below threshold a small diffusion current still flows, exponential in $V_{GS}$ like a BJT. But the gate controls the surface potential only through the divider $C_{ox}$–$C_{dep}$, so the exponent is $V_{GS}/nV_t$ with $n = 1 + C_{dep}/C_{ox} > 1$. The gate voltage needed per decade of current, the **subthreshold swing**, is therefore at least 59.6 mV at 300 K.

steps.prompt: A MOSFET has $C_{dep}/C_{ox}$ = {{r}} below threshold. Find its subthreshold swing at 300 K (gate voltage per decade of drain current).
With a thin enough gate oxide, a conventional MOSFET at 300 K can reach a subthreshold swing of 40 mV/decade.
steps.explanation: The subthreshold current is thermionic diffusion over a barrier, so it can change at most by a factor $e$ per $kT/q$: $S \ge (kT/q)\ln 10$ = 59.6 mV/decade, reached only when $C_{dep}/C_{ox} \to 0$. Beating it needs a different mechanism (e.g. tunnelling transistors) or cooling.

steps.prompt: A saturated NMOS transistor ($k'_n$ = {{kp}} µA/V², $W/L$ = {{WL}}) runs at an overdrive $V_{GS} - V_T$ = {{ov}} V. Find its transconductance $g_m$.
steps.explanation: $g_m = \partial I_D/\partial V_{GS}$ = $k'_n(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_T)$ = {{kp}} µA/V² × {{WL}} × {{ov}} V = **{{kp*1e-6*WL*ov|S}}**. Equivalently $g_m = 2I_D/(V_{GS} - V_T)$ with $I_D$ = {{0.5*kp*1e-6*WL*ov^2|A}}.

steps.prompt: In saturation a MOSFET carries {{I1||4}} mA at $V_{GS}$ = 1.2 V and {{I2||4}} mA at $V_{GS}$ = 1.8 V. Find its threshold voltage.
steps.explanation: $\sqrt{I_D} = \sqrt{K}(V_{GS} - V_T)$ is linear in $V_{GS}$. √{{I1||4}} = {{sqrt(I1)||4}} and √{{I2||4}} = {{sqrt(I2)||4}}. The line through both points reaches zero at $V_T = \frac{1.2\sqrt{I_2} - 1.8\sqrt{I_1}}{\sqrt{I_2} - \sqrt{I_1}}$ = **{{VT|V}}**. This $\sqrt{I_D}$ extrapolation is the standard way to measure $V_T$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $\sqrt{I_D}$ of a saturated MOSFET against $V_{GS}$. Read its threshold voltage.
steps.explanation: Extend the straight part of the line down to $\sqrt{I_D}$ = 0: it hits the axis at $V_{GS}$ ≈ **{{VT|V}}**. (A real curve bends near $V_T$ because of subthreshold current, which is why the straight part is extrapolated.)

steps.prompt: At $V_{GS} = V_T$ = {{VT}} V a MOSFET carries 1 µA, and below threshold its swing is {{S}} mV/decade. Estimate the off-current at $V_{GS}$ = 0.
steps.explanation: Going from $V_T$ down to 0 V covers {{VT*1000}} mV / {{S}} mV = {{VT*1000/S||3}} decades. $I_{off}$ = 1 µA × $10^{-{{VT*1000/S||3}}}$ = **{{1e-6*10^(-VT/(S*1e-3))*1e12||3}} pA**. This is why $V_T$ cannot be scaled down freely: every 60–100 mV less threshold costs a decade more leakage.

steps.prompt: In a very short channel the electrons travel at $v_{sat} = 10^7$ cm/s, so $I_D \approx WC_{ox}v_{sat}(V_{GS} - V_T)$. Find $I_D$ for $W$ = {{W}} µm, $t_{ox}$ = {{t}} nm and $V_{GS} - V_T$ = {{ov}} V.
steps.explanation: $C_{ox}$ = {{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)|F/cm²}}. $I_D = WC_{ox}v_{sat}(V_{GS} - V_T)$ = {{W}}$\times10^{-4}$ cm × {{3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)|F/cm²}} × $10^7$ cm/s × {{ov}} V = **{{W*1e-4*3.4515e-13/(t*1e-7)*1e7*ov|A}}**: the inversion charge at the source moving at $v_{sat}$, independent of $L$ and linear in the overdrive.

steps.prompt: Match each short-channel effect with its description
pairs: Drain voltage lowers the source barrier
Source and drain depletion regions merge
steps.explanation: All of them appear when the channel length becomes comparable to the depletion widths of the source and drain junctions, or when the fields become so high that carriers stop following $v = \mu E$. Scaling rules shrink oxide thickness, junction depths and supply voltage together with $L$ to keep them in check.

steps.prompt: When velocity saturation dominates, a MOSFET's saturation current grows roughly in proportion to $(V_{GS} - V_T)$ rather than $(V_{GS} - V_T)^2$.
steps.explanation: With all carriers at $v_{sat}$, the current is just charge × velocity: $I_D \approx WC_{ox}(V_{GS} - V_T)v_{sat}$, linear in the overdrive, and no longer dependent on $L$. Long channels follow the square law.

steps.title: Minority carriers in the base
steps.body: In an npn transistor the base–emitter junction injects electrons into the base. With a base much thinner than the diffusion length the electron profile is a straight line from $n_{B0}e^{V_{BE}/V_t}$ to zero at the collector junction, so the collector current is a pure diffusion current. Its gain is limited by holes back-injected into the emitter ($\gamma$) and by recombination in the base ($\alpha_T$).

steps.prompt: An npn transistor has emitter area {{A}} cm², base doping $N_B$ = {{NB}} cm⁻³, neutral base width $x_B$ = {{xB}} µm and electron diffusion coefficient $D_B$ = {{DB}} cm²/s in the base. Find the saturation current $I_S$ in femtoamperes (answer in fA).
steps.explanation: $I_S = qAD_Bn_i^2/(N_Bx_B)$ = 1.602$\times10^{-19}$ × {{A}} × {{DB}} × 2.25$\times10^{20}$ / ({{NB}} × {{xB}}$\times10^{-4}$ cm) = **{{1.602e-19*A*DB*2.25e20/(NB*xB*1e-4)*1e15||3}} fA**. The product $N_Bx_B$ (the Gummel number) sets $I_S$: a thinner or lighter base gives more current at the same $V_{BE}$.

steps.prompt: An npn transistor has a short emitter ($N_E$ = {{NE}} cm⁻³, $x_E$ = {{xE}} µm, hole diffusion coefficient $D_E$ = 2 cm²/s) and a short base ($N_B$ = {{NB}} cm⁻³, $x_B$ = {{xB}} µm, $D_B$ = 10 cm²/s). Use $\gamma \approx 1/(1 + N_BD_Ex_B/N_ED_Bx_E)$.

ask.prompt: Find the emitter injection efficiency $\gamma$ (4 significant figures).
Find the current gain $\beta$ if the emitter injection efficiency were the only limitation.
ask.explanation: With $\alpha_0 = \gamma$: $\beta = \gamma/(1 - \gamma)$ = $N_ED_Bx_E/(N_BD_Ex_B)$ = 1 / {{r||3}} = **{{1/r||3}}**. A heavily doped emitter and lightly doped base keep the back-injected hole current small. (Real transistors reach far less: very heavy emitter doping narrows the band gap there, which raises $n_i^2$ and the back-injected hole current.)

steps.prompt: The base of an npn transistor is $x_B$ = {{xB}} µm wide and the electron diffusion length in it is $L_B$ = {{LB}} µm. Find the current gain $\beta$ if only recombination in the base limited it ($\alpha_0 = \alpha_T = 1/\cosh(x_B/L_B)$).
steps.explanation: $\alpha_T = 1/\cosh({{xB}}/{{LB}})$ = {{1/cosh(xB/LB)||6}}. $\beta = \alpha_T/(1 - \alpha_T)$ = $1/(\cosh(x_B/L_B) - 1)$ = **{{1/(cosh(xB/LB) - 1)||3}}**, close to $2L_B^2/x_B^2$ = {{2*LB^2/xB^2||3}}. Base transport rarely limits modern transistors; the emitter efficiency does.

steps.prompt: A transistor has $\gamma$ = {{g||4}}, $\alpha_T$ = {{aT||4}} and negligible junction recombination ($\delta$ = 1). Find $\beta$.
steps.explanation: $\alpha_0 = \gamma\alpha_T$ = {{g||4}} × {{aT||4}} = {{g*aT||6}}. $\beta = \alpha_0/(1 - \alpha_0)$ = **{{g*aT/(1 - g*aT)||3}}**. Note how sensitive $\beta$ is: the 'losses' $1 - \gamma$ and $1 - \alpha_T$ simply add, and $\beta \approx 1/(\text{total loss})$.

steps.prompt: The graph shows $I_C$ against $V_{CE}$ for three base currents. Extend the saturated (sloped) parts to the left: they meet at $V_{CE} = -V_A$. Read the Early voltage $V_A$.
steps.explanation: The dashed extrapolations meet on the $V_{CE}$ axis at about −{{VA}} V, so $V_A$ ≈ **{{VA|V}}**. The output resistance is $r_o = V_A/I_C$, e.g. {{VA|V}} / 2 mA = {{VA/2e-3|Ω}} at $I_C$ = 2 mA.

steps.prompt: Base-width modulation gives an Early voltage $V_A \approx qN_Bx_B/C'_{jC}$. Find $V_A$ for $N_B$ = {{NB}} cm⁻³, $x_B$ = {{xB}} µm and a collector-junction capacitance of {{Cj}} nF/cm².
steps.explanation: The base charge per area is $qN_Bx_B$ = 1.602$\times10^{-19}$ × {{NB}} × {{xB}}$\times10^{-4}$ = {{1.602e-19*NB*xB*1e-4|C/cm²}}. A change $dV_{CB}$ removes $C'_{jC}dV_{CB}$ of it, so $I_C \propto 1/Q'_B$ rises with relative slope $C'_{jC}/Q'_B$: $V_A = Q'_B/C'_{jC}$ = **{{1.602e-19*NB*xB*1e-4/(Cj*1e-9)|V}}**.

steps.prompt: Why is the emitter of a bipolar transistor doped much more heavily than the base?
options: So that the emitter current consists almost entirely of electrons injected into the base, giving an injection efficiency close to 1
To make the base–emitter breakdown voltage as high as possible
So that electrons recombine faster in the emitter
steps.explanation: The ratio of hole current (back into the emitter) to electron current (into the base) is about $N_BD_Ex_B/(N_ED_Bx_E)$. A heavily doped emitter makes this tiny, so $\gamma \to 1$ and $\beta$ is large. Heavy doping actually **lowers** the B–E breakdown voltage.

steps.prompt: Making the base of a bipolar transistor thinner increases both its current gain and its Early voltage.
steps.explanation: A thinner base improves $\gamma$ and $\alpha_T$, so $\beta$ rises. But it holds less charge $qN_Bx_B$, so the same widening of the collector depletion region changes $x_B$ relatively more: $V_A \approx qN_Bx_B/C'_{jC}$ **drops**. The product $\beta V_A$ is a classic trade-off.
